documents: Wang et al. 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL099022 (published paper, PDF, 9 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (printed 'n of 9', identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: however, spatially and temporally detailed information on the changes in ice phenology on a global scale does not exist

sequences.source_document: Wang et al. 2022, GRL, published paper

steps.action: Named the gap: field records are too sparse, and no spatially and temporally detailed global quantification of lake ice phenology change exists. The authors set out to build a lake-level database for 1900-2099.
steps.quote: spatially and temporally detailed information on the changes in ice phenology on a global scale does not exist

steps.action: Built a dual logistic regression model (DLRM) that fits freeze-up and break-up dates to daily 500-m MODIS MOD10A1 snow-cover time series, weighting each image by its cloud-free fraction.
steps.quote: We developed a dual logistic regression model (DLRM) to determine the ice phenologies for each lake

steps.action: Validated the DLRM phenology dates against in situ GLRIPD field records and against 10-m Sentinel-2 MSI imagery, with Montreal Lake as the worked example (Figure 1, Figure S1).
steps.quote: Validation showed that the MODIS detected lake phenological indicators agreed well with both field records

steps.action: Attributed the larger freeze-up discrepancies between in situ and satellite values to how lakes are defined and to inaccurate geolocation of the in situ data, not to the DLRM (Text S1).
steps.quote: could have resulted from their inconsistent definition of the lakes or inaccurate geographical information of in situ data

steps.action: Built a temperature-threshold simulation model for each lake, with a required temperature and a preceding-period length as parameters. The model assumes lake-specific features stay unchanged, so timing depends only on preceding temperatures.
steps.quote: we established simulation models for individual lakes

steps.action: Calibrated each lake's model parameters on the 20-year satellite-detected phenologies and ERA5-Land daily mean air temperature.
steps.quote: allow us to calibrate the model parameters for tens of thousands of lakes worldwide

steps.action: Checked that the lake-specific models reproduce observed freeze-up and break-up dates (in situ and satellite), and compared their performance with the generic Weyhenmeyer et al. (2011) model, which they outperformed (Figure S6).
steps.quote: The simulations using our lake-specific models showed better agreement

steps.action: Designed the lake sample from HydroLAKES with these criteria: area >1 km2, north of 23.5°N, a GSWO permanent-water mask, >3 valid pixels, at least ten ice years, and a standard deviation of preceding temperature <2°C. This left 30,063 lakes.
steps.quote: These criteria resulted in a total of 30,063 lakes across the Northern Hemisphere

steps.action: Applied the DLRM to all 30,063 lakes to derive yearly freeze-up, break-up and ice duration for 2001-2020 (Figure 2).
steps.quote: We applied the dual logistic regression model to each of the 30,063 selected lakes

steps.action: Ran the lake-specific models on bias-corrected ISIMIP2b temperatures from four GCMs. Runs covered the past (1900-1999) and the future (2021-2099) under RCP 2.6, 6.0 and 8.5, and the four-model mean was stored in the GLIP database.
steps.quote: we conducted similar future simulations under three different anthropogenic greenhouse gas emission scenarios

steps.action: Set the analysis: per-lake linear trends with t-tests, trends of annual global medians, and anomalies of 1900-1919 and 2080-2099 relative to 2001-2020. Lakes were defined as ice-free when more than 15 of 20 years had no ice.
steps.quote: the trends were represented as the slopes of the linear regressions for the lake ice phenologies

steps.action: Estimated present-period phenology and trends: median freeze-up DOY 294.5, break-up DOY 146.5, and ice duration 217.5 days. Significantly shortened duration in 9.5% of lakes outnumbered significantly prolonged duration in 1.2%, with strong spatial heterogeneity.
steps.quote: The number of lakes with a significantly shortened ice duration (n = 2,853, or 9.5%) was 7.7-fold greater

steps.action: Compared the spatial pattern of 2001-2020 ice trends with air temperature trends, for example October-November cooling in northeastern North America and break-up warming in Europe (Figure S7).
steps.quote: The distributions of lake ice trends between 2001 and 2020 demonstrated spatial agreements with the patterns in air temperature

steps.action: Tested the temperature-only premise by correlating rates of change in freeze-up and break-up with rates of change in preceding 15-day temperature (P < 0.01, Figure S8).
steps.quote: the changing rates of freeze-up and break-up were significantly correlated with the changing rates of the temperatures in the preceding 15-day period

steps.action: Estimated 20th-century global trends from the simulations: +2.2 (freeze-up), -1.9 (break-up) and -4.0 (duration) days per 100 years. These differed significantly from the present period (matched-pair t-test), and 6.0% of lakes showed increased duration.
steps.quote: lake ice experienced mild but statistically significant warming trends for all three lake ice phenologies

steps.action: Explained the local 20th-century ice increases (Rocky Mountains, Tibetan Plateau, Greenland) by regional cooling, citing the authors' own earlier mapping study (X. Wang et al., 2021).
steps.quote: such sporadic lake ice increases were due to the regional decreases in air temperatures in these regions

steps.action: Estimated RCP 8.5 changes: rates more than an order of magnitude above 20th-century rates, a 49.9-day loss in global median duration by 2080-2099, and permanent ice loss in 160 lakes (0.5%).
steps.quote: we expect a global median loss of 49.9 days by the end of the 21st century

steps.action: Compared the fraction of lakes losing ice permanently with the independent projection of Sharma et al. (2019), 0.4%, and found it similar.
steps.quote: this fraction is similar to the projection by Sharma et al. (2019)

steps.action: Estimated RCP 6.0 changes (duration anomaly -33.1 days) and RCP 2.6 changes (-17.9 days, rates similar to the 20th century, 19 versus 49 newly ice-free lakes). Change scales with emission severity.
steps.quote: the global median ice duration anomaly would be −17.9 days by the end of the 21st century

steps.action: Retained the claim of continuous global lake ice loss and of mitigation through emission control. The GLIP database is offered as baseline information for impact studies.
steps.quote: our GLIP database provides critical baseline information to assess these consequences of historical and future lake ice dynamics

tree.answer: Lake ice loss under warming is known from sparse long records; the global, lake-level pattern is not.
The present period (2001-2020) is observed by satellite through the DLRM; the past and future are not observable and are simulated.
Quantify trends and anomalies in freeze-up, break-up and duration for about 30,000 lakes over 1900-2099.
No rival explanations are stated; only a rival model (the generic Weyhenmeyer model) is compared.
Conditions are found, not set: climate forcing over archived satellite years and GCM scenarios.

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats across 20 years and about 30,000 lakes, which allows lake-specific calibration.
Validated against in situ records, Sentinel-2, a generic-model baseline and temperature-trend correlation; spread across four GCMs is shown.
Kept: continuous loss of lake ice, with magnitudes per period and per emission scenario.

end.claim: Global (Northern Hemisphere) lake ice shows continuous loss from 1900 to 2099: mild but significant 20th-century warming trends, continued warming in about 60% of lakes in 2001-2020, and a projected 49.9-day loss in median ice duration by 2080-2099 under RCP 8.5, much reduced under lower-emission scenarios.

decisive_move.sentence: Calibrating a temperature-threshold model for each lake on 20 years of satellite-derived phenology is what lets the record be extended to 1900-2099; without it there is no two-century claim.

gates.evidence: Action: data are archival (MODIS, ERA5-Land, ISIMIP2b) and were acquired without a guiding hypothesis. Claim: the DLRM and the lake models were validated against in situ records, Sentinel-2 and a generic baseline model, and trend significance was tested with t-tests; but the headline past and future estimates are model outputs with no independent test of the 1900-1999 reconstruction reported in the main text. Registration: none reported; the selection thresholds (SD <2°C, ten ice years, >15 of 20 ice-free years) are stated without saying they were fixed in advance.

imports.item: logistic regression (dual logistic model fitted to snow-cover time series)
Student's t-test and matched-pair t-test for trend significance
Google Earth Engine processing platform and data catalog

novelty_claims.quote: We provide the first spatially and temporally detailed quantification of the changes in global lake ice across two centuries (1900–2099).
We provide the first characterization of the changes in global lake ice phenology across two centuries (1900–2099) at lake level
our analysis contributes the first comprehensive insight into how future global lake ice phenology changes might be mitigated through greenhouse gas emission control

limits:
The supporting information (Text S1, Figures S1-S8, Table S1) was not supplied, so validation statistics, calibration details and the model comparison are known only from main-text summaries. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments thank two anonymous reviewers, so no review sequence could be coded.

The 1900-1999 simulations rest on the stated assumption that lake-specific features (depth, sediment heat flux, inflow) stay unchanged. The main text reports no independent check of the simulated past against century-long in situ records; inference: such a check may sit in Figure S6 but cannot be confirmed. Discrepancies against in situ freeze-up data are attributed to the reference data rather than tested.

The lake selection (preceding-temperature SD <2°C, ten or more ice years) favours lakes that fit the temperature-only model. Inference: this may bias the sample toward lakes the model fits well. No alternative thresholds are reported. The 'global' results cover only Northern Hemisphere lakes (67% of frozen-lake area). GCM uncertainty is shown only as a standard-deviation band across four models.

Sub-claims:
- Present-period trends are estimate_with_resolution, observed from MODIS.
- Attribution of spatial trend patterns to air temperature and to the North Atlantic Current is best_explanation, with no rivals stated.
- Mitigation through emission control is a scenario-conditional estimate_with_resolution.
- Agreement with the Sharma et al. (2019) ice-free fraction is a consistency check, not a test.

disagreements.support: The lake-specific models agreed better with observations than the generic latitude and temperature model calibrated on Swedish lakes (Figures S6g-S6i).
disagreements.quote: underscoring the importance of incorporating lake-specific features in lake ice simulation models

disagreements.target: In situ freeze-up records in the Global Lake and River Ice Phenology Database (B. Benson et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: Larger satellite-versus-in-situ freeze-up discrepancies are attributed to inconsistent lake definitions and inaccurate geolocation of the in situ data (Text S1), not to the DLRM.
disagreements.quote: inaccurate geographical information of in situ data, rather than uncertainties in our dual logistic [...]

alternatives_considered.chosen: Lake-specific temperature-threshold models calibrated per lake
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Generic lake ice phenology model of Weyhenmeyer et al. (2011), with air temperature and latitude as inputs
alternatives_considered.reason: Lake heat storage and heat transport are lake specific, so a generic model is limited; the lake-specific models showed better agreement

alternatives_considered.chosen: Mean of simulations driven by four ISIMIP2b GCMs (HadGEM2-ES, GFDL-ESM2M, IPSL-CM5A-LR, MIROC5)
